sections.history: Innambur lies on the edge of Kumbakonam, in the Chola heartland north of the Kaveri, and the Tevaram hymns know it as Tiruinnambar. The saints Appar and Sambandar sang of the Lord here, which makes it a Paadal Petra Sthalam, and local tradition holds that a brick shrine stood on the site even before their time. The present stone temple carries inscriptions of the Chola period, reported to name Rajaraja I, along with later records of the Vijayanagara rulers, and it has been kept in worship ever since. The name Ezhutharinathar, the Lord who knows letters, ties the place to learning, and the village is remembered as a sanctuary of the written word.
sections.architecture: The temple follows the Dravidian plan: a rectangle of two prakarams enclosing about an acre, entered from the east beneath a five-tiered rajagopuram, with walls surrounding every shrine. Unusually, there is no flagstaff of the kind most Tamil temples have. Ezhutharinathar, also called Aksharapureeswarar, presides in the sanctum. The goddess Sugantha Kundalambikai has her own south-facing shrine on the right of the eastern outer courtyard, and a separate shrine honours Nithya Kalyani, also known as Soundara Nayaki. The sacred tree of the temple is the shenbagam, the golden champak.
sections.legends: The temple's name comes from a story of the Lord's quiet kindness. An honest accountant, whom tradition names Sudharman, was summoned by the king, who demanded the accounts of the realm by morning. Overwhelmed, and certain he could not finish, the man took refuge in Shiva. The Lord came in the accountant's own form, wrote out the entire accounts without a fault and presented them to the king, who was wholly satisfied. The grateful devotee found his burden lifted, and the god has been called Ezhutharinathar ever since. Other traditions add that the sun god regained his strength here, that Airavata, the elephant of Indra, bathed in the temple pond and worshipped, and that the sage Agastya learned the subtleties of Tamil grammar from the Lord.
sections.festivals: The festival calendar is led by the Aipasi Annabishekam in October or November, when the Lord is bathed in cooked rice, and by the ten-day Purattasi Navaratri in September or October. Margazhi Tiruvadhirai in December or January and a Chithirai festival in April or May are also kept, and Maha Shivaratri draws the largest crowds of the year. Dates follow the Tamil calendar, so confirm them locally.
sections.experience: Innambur rewards a quiet village darshan. Pass beneath the five-tiered gopuram into the stone courtyards, bow before Ezhutharinathar in the sanctum, and then visit the goddess Sugantha Kundalambikai and the shrine of Nithya Kalyani. Because the Lord here is remembered as the keeper of letters, students and parents often come to pray for learning and a clear mind, and it is a natural place to offer a prayer before a child's first lessons. The temple lies a short way outside Kumbakonam among green Kaveri fields, and its courtyards hold a calm that suits a longer pause.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning (roughly 6 to 11 a.m.) and again in the evening (roughly 5 to 8 p.m.), with a midday break; listings differ, so confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Innambur is about 10 km from Kumbakonam on the Tiruvaiyaru road and is easily reached from Swamimalai. Kumbakonam, the nearest railway station, has regular buses to the village. Tiruchirappalli, with the region's airport, is the nearest air link, roughly 90 km away.
